metadata.research_goal: Create backend-ready boxing tactical knowledge covering range, rhythm, pressure, counterpunching, southpaw/orthodox matchups, ring generalship, feints, traps, corner adjustments, and level-based tactical IQ.

source_refs.title: Boxing
source_refs.notes: Used for scoring, ring, knockdown, and competition context.

key_concepts.summary: Long, mid, and inside range change punch selection, defense, footwork, and energy cost.
Boxers win exchanges by changing rhythm, timing entries, breaking opponent rhythm, and varying tempo.
Controlling space, exits, and where exchanges happen is a scoring and safety skill.
Out-boxer, pressure fighter, counterpuncher, boxer-puncher, and inside fighter profiles create different training demands.
Open-stance matchups change lead-foot battle, jab lanes, rear-hand line, and outside angle priorities.
Between-round tactical adjustments should become teachable decision rules for the app.

tactical_rules.rule: Combinations should end with guard return, angle, step-out, clinch, or defensive responsibility.
Pressure is not chasing; teach angle cutting and exit denial before high-volume pressure rounds.
Counterpunching drills need a specific trigger: jab, cross, lazy return, predictable step, or overcommit.
Intermediate and advanced athletes should use feints to collect reactions before entries.
Open-stance work should teach lead-foot position, rear-hand line, and outside angle without overloading beginners.
If ahead, prioritize clean scoring, exits, and risk control; if behind, increase initiative without reckless exchanges.

physical_demands.quality: short burst entry and exit speed
visual processing, trunk movement, and head movement timing
sustain footwork and punch volume without technical collapse
trunk, shoulder, forearm, and neck robustness

injury_or_load_risks.risk: Tactical immaturity can increase unnecessary head contact.
High-pressure rounds can create fatigue-based guard errors.
Inside work and clinch-like contact increase neck and shoulder load.
Southpaw/orthodox matchups can increase foot clashes and balance disruptions.
Counterpunching drills can escalate contact if constraints are not clear.

training_implications.summary: Use style archetypes to build specific tactical problems, not labels for identity.
Tactical skills should progress through constrained rounds before open sparring.
Tactical learning can happen with touch sparring, pads, shadow, and partner drills.
Use ahead/behind/even/hurt/tired scenarios for match IQ training.
Future user progress should store recurring tactical issues and successful solutions.
